abstract: Dr. Greuel's lecture covers the practical use of transvaginal ultrasound in a family medicine setting, including patient communication, proper setup, and scanning technique. Key topics include distinguishing true gestational sacs from pseudosacs using the double decidual sign, measuring mean sac diameter and crown-rump length, and recognizing ectopic pregnancy with free fluid in the cul-de-sac. The talk emphasizes systematic scanning to avoid missing twins or adnexal pathology, and provides guidance on when to repeat studies or refer for formal ultrasound.
key_points: Obtain informed consent by explaining the procedure, including the use of a condom-covered probe and the possibility of needing a formal ultrasound later.
Perform transvaginal ultrasound with an empty bladder; the probe is inserted along the posterior vaginal wall and advanced slowly while looking for the uterus.
Orient the probe with the marker to the patient's right (your left) for transverse views; the left side of the screen corresponds to the patient's anterior.
Systematically scan the uterus from side to side in both longitudinal and transverse planes to avoid missing twins, heterotopic pregnancy, or ovarian cysts.
A true gestational sac is rounded or elliptical in two planes, eccentric to the endometrial stripe, and shows a double decidual sign; a pseudogestational sac lacks these features.
Mean sac diameter is calculated from three orthogonal measurements; crown-rump length is the average of three measurements from the top of the head to the bottom of the buttocks.
If no fetal pole is seen at 6 weeks, consider anembryonic gestation (blighted ovum) and repeat ultrasound in one week with ectopic precautions.
Switch from crown-rump length to Hadlock fetal biometry at 14 weeks gestation.
Free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac raises concern for ruptured ectopic pregnancy or infection, especially when no intrauterine pregnancy is seen.
Pregnancy of undetermined location should be treated as ectopic until an intrauterine gestational sac is definitively identified.
Absence of a yolk sac by the end of 6 weeks is abnormal.
No cardiac activity by the middle of the 6th week is a concerning finding.
